en: A Treatise on the Biography of the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, composed by Liang Su of Anding. The Treatise states:
Those who cultivate the teachings of the Śākya clan focus on three things alone: namely, precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). This Way... at its beginning...
From the initial aspiration for enlightenment to the attainment of wondrous awakening, it weaves through the three vehicles and guides all myriad practices until its purpose is fully realized.
In the past, when the Dharma King appeared in the world, he relied upon the single path of purity and employed a single voice to preach;

yet because the capacities and responses of sentient beings differed, what they heard was likewise diverse. Thus, there arose the meanings of the five periods and five flavors, the provisional and the real, the partial and the complete, the small and the great.
Disseminated across the various schools, these teachings appear as distinct streams; yet, when one examines their ultimate destination, they do not transcend the Single Reality.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Though various paths are taught, their reality is but the Buddha-vehicle. It also says: "Opening the gate of skillful means to reveal the mark of truth.

This is illustrated by the metaphor of myriad rivers flowing into the sea and signified by the Gate of Non-duality. Both self and others attain [enlightenment] together, arriving at the same secret treasury.
This is the reason for the composition of this Esoteric Teaching. Since the extinction at the Crane Forest (Kuśinagara), the net of the Dharma has been dispersed;
since the power of the divine feet (ṛddhipāda) was concealed, the paths of the schools have diverged. Each authority relies on its own provisional standpoint, resulting in mutual contradictions.

Furthermore, because the manifestations of birth through samādhi and the appearances of the Four Reliances (catur-śaraṇa) vary according to the capacities of beings, their tenets and treatises also differ. Thus, there arose the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Tattvasiddhi*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Categorizing and dividing the paths, they simultaneously engaged in discourses of "neither existence nor emptiness," unable to achieve a unified consistency.
As they moved further from the Sage, this trend increasingly flourished. Those who expounded the Dharma were shackled by words and knew not how to liberate themselves;

those who practiced Chan rendered the nature and characteristics of phenomena void, making them impossible to draw back to reality. Thus, those who held to this rejected that, and those who had not yet realized claimed to have attained wisdom.
As the Way of liberation flowed outward, people forgot their physical bodies and neglected the affairs of body and speech;
their conduct became dissolute and lacked discipline, such that the great tradition of the Dharma gate was nearly extinguished. Subsequently, the teaching did not remain in perpetual decline;

the Tathāgatas Huiwen and Huisi appeared in succession, leaping forth like dragons. Yet, as the thunder of the Dharma had not yet reached all quarters, the wooden clapper was once again entrusted to Tiantai.

The Great Master’s image surpasses that of Śāriputra and Subhūti in its transcendent awakening; it possesses the auspicious marks (or, according to another version, the marks of virtue, or extraordinary manifestations) of Emperor Yao and the Great Shun.

It extols the bequeathed treatises of Nāgārjuna and follows the subtle understanding of Mount Nanyue. Thereafter, by employing the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it establishes the causal conditions for a single matter;
it encompasses the myriad dharmas within the one mind and unfolds the ten vehicles through the eight teachings. Thus is the precept [established].
The discourse on samādhi and prajñā, and the contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way, are now utterly clear and can be put into practice.

Thus, there is no teaching left untransmitted, no dharma abandoned, no person neglected, and no mind not engaged; conduct is without discrimination, and through this conduct, realization is attained, each with its own lineage.
It is for this reason that the Great Master’s school flourishes, and while he was in the world, his light illuminated the whole realm.
He served as a teacher and model for emperors and kings; upon his passing from this world, he traveled to the upper realms to serve as an assistant to Maitreya.

Manifesting through the universal gate (*samantamukha*), he displayed his transformative virtues as an envoy of the Tathāgata. His stages of attainment, rank, objective realm, and wisdom are beyond all description. Alas!
Though his manifested traces have departed, his subtle words have not fallen into ruin; those who practice them are still sufficient to withstand and refute [all opposition].

The hundred schools clearly manifest the Three Baskets; how much more so for one who hears them and is able to contemplate, contemplates and is able to practice, practices and is able to advance, and advances without ceasing?
Regarding such a person, even if they have not yet attained realization, I must say they are close to it. Among people today, those with correct faith are rare;
those who open the gate of Chan sometimes claim there is neither Buddha nor Dharma, and ask what sin or virtue there can be.
Within this process of transformation, those of inferior capacity—those who gallop after greed and craving, and those who move within the ranks of the gentry and officials—deem these words ultimate;

for they do not offend the ear and do not obstruct private desires, so those who follow their path are like birds flying toward a bright lamp or clods of earth falling into a deep valley. Little do they realize that they are being brought to a state of scorching and burning.
Unable to emerge from it themselves, though they wish to benefit others, they actually cause them harm; their infliction of injury is identical to that of the various māras and non-Buddhists.
Viewed from this perspective, the great precepts of this school and the auxiliary salvation of this teaching are incomparable to anything else in the world.
Since the Dharma was transmitted by the Master Zhi (Jizang) through five generations until the present, it has been revitalized by the Great Master Zhanran.
Since Dao gave me this account, I have recorded it and appended it to this chapter. Liang Su, courtesy name Jingzhi, was a native of Anding (Note:

according to the *Liu Wen* commentary, his original style was Kuangzhong; he was the fifth-generation descendant of Bei, the Minister of Justice during the Sui dynasty, and his family had resided in Binhun for generations).

From an early age, he followed the teachings of the Śākya clan and transmitted the Tiantai school’s doctrines from Jingxi, serving as a disciple with great reverence, his resolve being fixed upon a single goal.

Because the *Zhengfa nianchu jing zhong wenda* (Questions and Answers on the Scripture on the Contemplation of Mindfulness of the Correct Dharma) is the most refined and extensive [of his works], the Patriarchal Lineage of Gushan states:

"Among those in the imperial court who attained the Way, there was only the single person, Master Liang. The Master once edited and finalized the *Tiantai Zhi guan* (Contemplation and Practice) into six fascicles for circulation in the world (*Fozu tongji* states:

"Because the text and meaning of the *Zhi guan* were so vast and profound that readers would spend excessive days upon them, he therefore edited and finalized it into six fascicles"). He also composed the *Zhi guan tong li* (General Principles of Contemplation and Practice), the style of which is majestic.

Profound, elegant, vigorous, and refined, it follows the steps of the *Appended Judgments* of the *Book of Changes* and the *Doctrine of the Mean*. (The *Fozu Tongji* states that he further composed a "General Preface" appended at the end, asserting that the *Zhi Guan* is a work for saving the world and clarifying the Way;

he also wrote a "Biographical Discourse on the Great Master," providing a comprehensive account of the great lineage of the transmission of the teachings. It is said that as for its style, it is majestic, profound, elegant, and vigorous; as for its principles, they are clear and penetrating.
Although Han Changli was peerless during the Yuanhe era, when compared with [the works from] Wuyuan and his other writings, he seems not to have surpassed him. — Tang Dynasty.
The histories state that during the Dali and Zhenyuan eras, many scholars favored the study of antiquity, yet only the Master was renowned for his profound depth.
Han Yu associated with his disciples, applying himself with keen intent to their emulation and seeking to establish himself as a preeminent figure of his generation;
from this, one may discern the origins of Han’s literary style. Furthermore, Liu Zhitou’s "Record of Former Friends" also praised him as being most capable of composing prose. Moreover—

Cui Gong composed the preface for the "Epitaph for the Tiantai Jingxi [Zhiyi]," stating: "He who knew the essentials of the Dharma and discerned the provisional and the real composed the 'Stele for Chanlin Monastery on Mount Tiantai';
he who reached the source of the teachings and employed the principles of object and wisdom composed the 'Stele for the Great Master of Jingxi.
To this day, among the epigraphic texts of the Shanjia school, these two steles alone stand as the preeminent. The Master’s collected works comprise twenty fascicles.
Regrettably, the woodblocks for his work have worn away and there is no one to re-publish them.
Kaian once beheld a manuscript at Beifeng that bore the personal postscript and praise of the Master of Non-Action, Yang Jie; his admiration was boundless.

He passed away in Chang’an in the eleventh month of the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of forty-three. Duke Cui remarked, "The court honors virtue, and therefore it appointed you [to office]."
As the Crown Prince’s tutor, you served as the Director of the National Archives; thus, you were appointed as a Compiler in the History Bureau.

As the one who issued edicts and spread the royal governance, you were appointed as a Scholar of the Hanlin Academy. Since these three offices were simultaneously established for you, your position at court cannot be said to be one of failure.
Having passed the age of forty, you are revered by the scholarly community, comparable to Yan Hui and Huang Shudu.

"It is not that he did not live a long life; as for those mediocre men who grow old in the office of the Langshu, with white hair in the world of men, what benefit could they possibly provide? (Shimen Zhengtong).

According to the preface by Cui Gong of Hedong to the collected works of the Liang family, it is said that "all the compositions of the Śākya school are refined, beautiful, profound, and far-reaching."

In this world, there is nothing that can rival the *Sōmyōkyōhonron* (Treatise on the Grades of the Teaching of the Clear and High). It states: "The prose of Chen Zi'ang is not equal to that of Li Hua;
the prose of Li Hua is not equal to that of Liang Su. In the writings of Liang Su, the gentleman may find something to adopt.

Regarding the narration of Liang's life and deeds, none is more detailed than the *Shimen Zhengtong* (Orthodox Lineage of the Buddhist Gate). Consequently, while I was collating and editing the *Zhi Guan*, I have set forth [this work].
Furthermore, I have appended one or two critical evaluations from later scholars;
if you read these, you will understand Xu’s approach to learning and composition, so what more need I say?
A Letter from Genshō of Sōzan, dated the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Kōbun era.
